scenarios.title: Development persistent-mount workspace fixture
scenarios.summary: Unbundled development fixture; not authored curriculum or objective coverage.
scenarios.objective: The work filesystem is UUID 11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111. Repair its saved source, attach it writable at /work and make it survive the independent device-name tests. Keep reports (UUID 22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222) at /reports read-only and automatic, with its final live mount intact. Keep the supplied dump/check fields. Save file edits, inspect the live mounts and check the complete configuration.
scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare the saved source and current live state. A valid file alone does not create a live mount.
steps: Mount and verify current and saved behavior
scenarios.explanation: The work UUID identifies the intended volume even when its connection name changes. Saving repaired the persistent instruction; mounting made it live. Reports retained its identity and read-only policy in both sessions.
hints: Compare the work UUID with the available inventory.
Saving and validation do not create a live mount.
Test copies change device names; a current /dev source can point to a different same-type volume.
scenarios.simplifications: Pure clean-volume metadata and bounded literal terminal commands only; no disk blocks, files, actual mount, boot, systemd, privilege or filesystem repair. Validate configuration and Test saved mounts are simulator actions. Native integration fixture only, unbundled/not counted.

storage_teaching.prerequisite_note: Assumes basic Linux paths and typing a command. This lesson introduces mountpoints, filesystem identities and saved versus live mount settings. You can reopen this introduction or skip to the complete assignment.

concepts.title: Attach a filesystem to a directory
concepts.text: A mount makes a filesystem available at a directory called a mountpoint. The activity supplies clean simulated volumes. It does not create a disk or change anything on your computer.

concepts.title: Use the identity from the ticket
concepts.text: The ticket tells you which UUID belongs to each role. blkid lists the available UUIDs and filesystem types. A /dev name is a current connection name; it can change. A filesystem UUID identifies the same volume across the controlled name changes in this exercise.

concepts.title: Saved instructions and live mounts are separate
concepts.text: Each saved line has six fields: source, mountpoint, type, options, dump and check. rw means writable; ro means read-only. Keep the last two supplied numbers: this simulator stores them without running backups or checks. Save stores the file; Validate checks it without mounting. A mount command attaches the saved entry. Test saved mounts tries independent copies with changed device names, not a real system boot.

storage_teaching.example_description: In this separate example, practice work is UUID aaaaaaaa-aaaa-4aaa-8aaa-aaaaaaaaaaa1 at /practice-work. Keep practice reports at /practice-reports read-only. Fill worked example supplies only this example file; save it, inspect it and mount the work target yourself.

fixture.configuration:
UUID=aaaaaaaa-aaaa-4aaa-8aaa-aaaaaaaaaaa9 /practice-work ext4 rw 0 2
UUID=aaaaaaaa-aaaa-4aaa-8aaa-aaaaaaaaaaa2 /practice-reports ext4 ro 0 2

example_commands.explanation: List simulated device names, UUIDs and types; compare them with the ticket. This does not discover a volume’s business purpose.
Read the saved file. The editor may still contain unsaved changes.
Attach the volume named by the saved /practice-work entry. This command succeeds only after its source is repaired and saved.
List the live mounts and their read-only or writable policy. Listing them does not change them.

storage_teaching.try_change: After solving the example, replace its work source with /dev/practice1, save and test again. It works with today’s names but selects the wrong volume in the swapped test copy. Restore the UUID to repair it. Your assignment stays unchanged.
